meta.notes: Quality-expanded set: weak filler removed; added scenario-based questions with realistic traps, per-option explanations, quick examples, and official Databricks source links.

questions.question: A Generative AI Engineer is loading 150 million embeddings into a vector database that takes a maximum of 100 million. Which TWO actions can they take to reduce the record count?

options.text: Increase the document chunk size
options.explanation: Correct. A larger chunk size means each vector row represents more text, so the same corpus usually creates fewer chunks and fewer embeddings. Example: 1,000 pages split into 1,000-token chunks creates fewer rows than splitting them into 250-token chunks.

options.text: Decrease the overlap between chunks
options.explanation: Correct. Lower overlap reduces duplicated text between adjacent chunks, which reduces the number of chunks and vector rows. Example: moving from 200-token overlap to 40-token overlap can keep continuity while reducing duplicated embeddings.

options.text: Decrease the document chunk size
options.explanation: Incorrect. Smaller chunks normally increase the number of chunks and embeddings. Example: splitting each policy section into sentence-sized chunks usually creates many more index records.

options.text: Increase the overlap between chunks
options.explanation: Incorrect. More overlap duplicates content across chunks and usually increases the record count. Example: 50% overlap can almost double the number of chunks compared with no overlap.

options.text: Use a smaller embedding model
options.explanation: Incorrect. A smaller embedding model may reduce vector dimension and storage per row, but it does not reduce how many rows/chunks are inserted. Example: switching 1024-dim to 384-dim embeddings changes vector size, not chunk count.

questions.explanation: This is about record count, not vector size. Record count is mainly controlled by how many chunks you create: larger chunks and less overlap produce fewer records.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A customer-facing automotive parts app can answer order and billing details using account_id and transaction_id, but fails on shipping and expected arrival dates. Which approach would improve this?

options.text: Create a vector store with company shipping policies and payment terms for all parts
options.explanation: Incorrect. Policy text may explain general shipping rules, but the question requires transaction-specific expected arrival dates. Example: a policy saying “standard shipping is 3-5 days” cannot answer order 123’s actual carrier ETA.

options.text: Create a feature store table with transaction_id as primary key populated with invoice data and expected delivery date
options.explanation: Correct. The app already has transaction_id, and expected delivery date is structured, transaction-level data; a keyed table is the right source. Example: lookup transaction_id=TX123 and return its invoice status plus expected_delivery_date.

options.text: Fine-tune periodically on example expected arrival dates
options.explanation: Incorrect. Fine-tuning is poor for frequently changing, record-specific facts. Example: a model fine-tuned yesterday still would not know today’s updated ETA for one order.

options.text: Prompt the model to add 14 days to the order date
options.explanation: Incorrect. A hard-coded date rule will be wrong for different carriers, regions, inventory status, and exceptions. Example: overnight shipping or delayed shipments would both be misrepresented.

questions.explanation: The missing knowledge is structured and keyed by transaction. Use the source that contains the actual field, rather than hoping a prompt or fine-tune recreates operational data.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A RAG application uses scanned source documents saved as image files such as .jpeg or .png. The engineer wants the least code to extract text. Which Python package should be used?

options.text: beautifulsoup
options.explanation:
Incorrect. BeautifulSoup parses HTML/XML, not pixels in scanned image files. Example: it works for

text

in a webpage, not a photographed invoice.

options.text: scrapy
options.explanation: Incorrect. Scrapy is a web-crawling framework; it can fetch pages but does not perform OCR on images. Example: use Scrapy to collect pages, then OCR would still be needed for scanned images.

options.text: pytesseract
options.explanation: Correct. pytesseract is a Python wrapper for Tesseract OCR and is suitable for extracting text from image files. Example: use it to read text from a scanned PNG of a contract page.

options.text: pyquery
options.explanation: Incorrect. pyquery is for jQuery-like querying of HTML/XML documents, not optical character recognition. Example: it can select div elements, but it cannot read text from a JPEG scan.

questions.explanation: Scanned image documents require OCR. HTML parsers and crawlers are useful for web pages, but not for image-only text extraction.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: Documents for a retriever are chunked to a maximum of 512 tokens. Cost and latency are more important than quality. Which embedding model context-length option best fits?

options.text: context length 512: smallest model is 0.13GB and embedding dimension 384
options.explanation: Correct. The chunks fit within 512 tokens, and the smallest model/dimension best matches the cost-latency priority. Example: for 512-token FAQ chunks, a compact embedding model can be enough and cheaper to serve.

options.text: context length 514: smallest model is 0.44GB and embedding dimension 768
options.explanation: Incorrect. It also fits, but it is larger than necessary for a scenario prioritizing cost and latency. Example: paying for a larger vector when your chunks are already within 512 tokens is unnecessary unless quality demands it.

options.text: context length 2048: smallest model is 11GB and embedding dimension 2560
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is over-sized for 512-token chunks and increases compute/storage cost. Example: a 2048-token context model is useful for longer chunks, not short snippets with strict latency needs.

options.text: context length 32768: smallest model is 14GB and embedding dimension 4096
options.explanation: Incorrect. Very long context and high dimensionality are excessive for short chunks and cost/latency constraints. Example: this would be a poor fit for a lightweight help-center retriever.

questions.explanation: Match embedding context length to chunk size and optimization objective. If quality is not the priority, avoid over-sized models and dimensions.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: An engineer wants to update a paragraph-long memo into a single-sentence gist that fits into a front end. Which NLP task category should they evaluate LLMs for?

options.text: text2text Generation
options.explanation: Incorrect. Text-to-text is broad and can include many transformations, but the specific requirement is compressing content into a shorter gist. Example: translation is also text-to-text but would not solve memo summarization.

options.text: Sentencizer
options.explanation: Incorrect. A sentencizer splits text into sentences; it does not generate a concise gist. Example: it can identify sentence boundaries in a paragraph, not rewrite the paragraph into one sentence.

options.text: Text Classification
options.explanation: Incorrect. Classification assigns labels, not a rewritten summary. Example: classifying a memo as “complaint” or “request” is not the same as producing a one-sentence gist.

options.text: Summarization
options.explanation: Correct. The task is to reduce a longer text into a shorter representation that preserves the key intent. Example: turn a 200-word support note into “Customer requests a refund for a delayed shipment.”

questions.explanation: The desired output is a concise summary, not a label or a sentence-boundary operation.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: An online retailer has 100 million inventory items, around 80 searches per second, and latency is critical. The team accepts upfront development cost if it improves accuracy without harming latency. How should vector search be configured?

options.text: Use GTE Large, standard vector search, hybrid search and reranking on
options.explanation: Incorrect. Hybrid search and reranking can improve relevance, but reranking adds extra processing; standard index type may not be ideal at very large scale. Example: reranking top candidates can be useful for support docs but may hurt strict high-QPS latency.

options.text: Use GTE Large, storage optimized vector search, hybrid search and reranking on
options.explanation: Incorrect. Storage optimized helps large indexes, but reranking still adds latency and a generic embedding may not be best when the team can invest upfront. Example: reranking every retail search can be too slow at 80 QPS.

options.text: Fine tune a custom embedding model, use standard vector search, keep hybrid search and reranking off
options.explanation: Correct. The answer key emphasizes optimizing embedding quality upfront while avoiding query-time features that add latency. Example: a product-domain embedding model can improve nearest-neighbor quality without adding a reranker call on every query.

options.text: Fine tune a custom embedding model, use storage optimized vector search, keep hybrid search and reranking off
options.explanation: Incorrect. Storage optimized may help very large embedding counts, but the official sample answer selects standard vector search with custom embeddings for this latency-critical setup. Example: choose index type based on Databricks size/latency guidance, not only raw item count.

questions.explanation: This official sample tests the tradeoff between upfront model/index work and query-time latency. The exam answer is the custom embedding approach without hybrid/reranking overhead.

questions.question: A team needs gated prompt promotion from dev to staging to prod, version history, and rollback. Which approach supports this?

options.text: Store prompt templates in the app repo and promote by branch merges
options.explanation: Incorrect. Git can version files, but the exam objective is Databricks/MLflow prompt lifecycle management with aliases and model/application tracking. Example: a branch merge alone does not give runtime prompt aliases like champion/staging.

options.text: Track prompts as MLflow versions and promote using aliases after they pass
options.explanation: Correct. Versioned prompts plus aliases support gated promotion and rollback. Example: promote a tested prompt to a production alias after evaluation passes, then roll back the alias if quality drops.

options.text: Save prompts in JSON on the CI runner and overwrite prod on each run
options.explanation: Incorrect. Overwriting on CI loses clean version history and rollback semantics. Example: after a bad deployment, you may not know which previous prompt text was stable.

options.text: Put prompts in Delta tables and overwrite the prod table every deployment
options.explanation: Incorrect. Delta can store prompt text, but overwriting production rows is not a full prompt lifecycle/promotion workflow. Example: it does not by itself provide tested aliases for app versions.

questions.explanation: For exam prep, think “version, evaluate, promote, rollback” rather than “copy/overwrite text.”
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A Databricks App lets support agents ask questions grounded in PDFs. Users must authenticate with corporate identity; the app must call an agent endpoint without exposing long-lived browser tokens; answers must respect user permissions. Which approach fits?

options.text: Use a Databricks App backend to call the Agent endpoint with app credentials and enforce user identity/permissions via the app authenticated context
options.explanation: Correct. The backend keeps credentials away from browser JavaScript and can enforce the authenticated user context. Example: the app backend calls the agent endpoint while checking the user’s groups before retrieving restricted docs.

options.text: Store a PAT in JavaScript and call the Agent endpoint directly
options.explanation: Incorrect. A browser-visible PAT is a serious credential leak risk. Example: anyone opening DevTools could copy the token and call the endpoint outside the app.

options.text: Publish the endpoint publicly and protect it with an API key in the frontend
options.explanation: Incorrect. A frontend API key is still exposed to users and does not provide per-user corporate identity controls. Example: one leaked key could allow access by unauthorized users.

options.text: Export PDFs to a public bucket so the Agent can read them without identity checks
options.explanation: Incorrect. This bypasses governance and can leak internal content. Example: salary policy PDFs should not become publicly readable just to simplify retrieval.

questions.explanation: Serving an enterprise GenAI app requires authentication, backend credential handling, and permission-aware retrieval.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A research assistant agent needs a managed Databricks MCP server for one internet data source and an external MCP server for an API requiring a key. Which TWO actions should the engineer take?

options.text: Build one custom MCP server wrapping both resources
options.explanation: Incorrect. A custom server increases maintenance and ignores the available managed server. Example: do not build your own web-search wrapper if Databricks already provides a managed MCP integration for that source.

options.text: Use the managed web browser MCP server to programmatically navigate internet resources
options.explanation: Incorrect. Browser automation is not the same as configuring the specific managed MCP server identified by the platform. Example: use the managed server identifier rather than brittle page navigation.

options.text: Cache all resources and search results as Unity Catalog external tables
options.explanation: Incorrect. Caching may help some workloads, but it does not integrate live managed/external MCP tools. Example: web search results and API responses may need fresh calls, not a stale table.

options.text: Configure the managed MCP server by specifying type managed and its server identifier
options.explanation: Correct. This uses the managed server with lower maintenance. Example: add the Databricks-managed server to the agent MCP configuration rather than hosting it yourself.

options.text: Deploy the external MCP server with connection details, store the API key in Databricks Secrets, and reference it in configuration
options.explanation: Correct. External tools need secure connection and secret handling. Example: put the API key in a secret scope instead of hardcoding it in agent code.

questions.explanation: Use managed integrations when available, and secure external integrations with secrets/configuration rather than hardcoded credentials.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: Domain experts rate customer-support RAG answers weekly, but ratings vary widely for the same responses. What should the engineer do to create a dependable evaluation process?

options.text: Use an LLM-as-judge as the primary source of truth instead of experts
options.explanation: Incorrect. LLM judges can scale evaluation, but expert disagreement should be resolved with rubrics/calibration rather than discarded. Example: for legal policy answers, SMEs define what “complete” means before judge alignment.

options.text: Define clear rubrics, calibrate SMEs, and use aligned judgments in mlflow.genai.evaluate()
options.explanation: Correct. Rubrics reduce rater inconsistency and create a more reliable evaluation set. Example: define separate criteria for factuality, completeness, citation quality, and actionability before SMEs score.

options.text: Average all scores and treat the blended score as definitive
options.explanation: Incorrect. Averaging hides disagreement but does not fix inconsistent criteria. Example: two experts scoring 1 and 5 average to 3, but that does not tell you what the app should improve.

options.text: Keep only responses where all experts already agree
options.explanation: Incorrect. Removing disputed examples can make the evaluation set too easy and unrepresentative. Example: ambiguous refund-policy cases are exactly where the app needs robust evaluation.

questions.explanation: For human feedback, align the rubric first. Good evaluation depends on consistent criteria, not just more labels.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A business wants an assistant that answers HR-policy questions using frequently updated PDF documents and must cite the source section. Which design best matches the requirement?

options.text: RAG pipeline: ingest and chunk PDFs, index chunks, retrieve relevant chunks, then generate an answer with citations
options.explanation: Correct. RAG keeps frequently updated documents outside the model weights and can pass retrieved source chunks into the prompt. Example: when the parental-leave PDF changes, re-index the document rather than retraining the LLM.

options.text: Fine-tune the LLM monthly on all HR PDFs and ask it to remember the source sections
options.explanation: Incorrect. Fine-tuning is not the best pattern for frequently changing factual documents or citations. Example: the model may still answer from stale weights after a policy update.

options.text: Use an embedding model by itself to generate the final natural-language answer
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embedding models produce vectors for similarity search; they do not generate final user-facing prose. Example: embed the question to retrieve the leave-policy chunk, then pass it to a chat model.

options.text: Use only a SQL dashboard because PDFs are unstructured documents
options.explanation: Incorrect. SQL dashboards are useful for structured analytics, but they do not by themselves answer free-form policy questions from PDFs. Example: HR PDFs need extraction/chunking before retrieval.

questions.explanation: This tests mapping business requirements to a pipeline. Frequent document updates + citations usually points to RAG, not memorization in model weights.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: An LLM must classify support messages and return exactly JSON with fields ticket_id, category, and confidence. Which prompt is strongest?

options.text: Classify this ticket.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is underspecified: it does not define the output schema or allowed categories. Example: the model might respond in prose instead of JSON.

options.text: Return JSON only with keys ticket_id, category, confidence. category must be one of Billing, Login, Shipping, Other. Use null if a field is missing.
options.explanation: Correct. It defines format, allowed labels, and missing-value behavior. Example: {"ticket_id":"T1","category":"Billing","confidence":0.82}.

options.text: Please be concise and helpful when answering the support team.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Tone instructions do not enforce structured extraction/classification. Example: the response may be short but still not parseable JSON.

options.text: Summarize the ticket and then maybe include a category if obvious.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This asks for a summary, not strict classification. Example: a downstream parser could fail if the model returns paragraphs.

questions.explanation: For formatted outputs, specify exact schema, allowed values, and constraints. The exam often rewards precise output contracts.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A team wants the fastest Databricks-managed way to create a document-grounded chatbot over internal PDFs with citations. Which Agent Bricks capability is the best fit?

options.text: Knowledge Assistant
options.explanation: Correct. Knowledge Assistant is intended for creating high-quality chatbots over a document knowledge base and can provide cited answers. Example: point it at policy documents and use the resulting endpoint in a support app.

options.text: Information Extraction
options.explanation: Incorrect. Information Extraction is for extracting structured fields from unstructured text, not primarily for open-ended document QA. Example: extracting invoice_number and total from invoices is IE.

options.text: Supervisor Agent
options.explanation: Incorrect. Supervisor Agent coordinates multiple specialized agents/tools; it is more appropriate when several agents or tools must be orchestrated. Example: route a question between Genie, a web-search tool, and a ticketing API.

options.text: AI Gateway rate limits
options.explanation: Incorrect. Rate limits control consumption on serving endpoints; they do not build a document-grounded chatbot. Example: cap a team at 50 queries per minute after the app exists.

questions.explanation: Pick the managed capability that directly matches the use case. Document-grounded Q&A with citations maps to Knowledge Assistant.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A finance team receives vendor contracts and wants structured fields such as renewal_date, termination_notice_days, and governing_law. Which Databricks capability best matches the task?

options.text: Information Extraction
options.explanation: Correct. The goal is to extract structured fields from unstructured contracts. Example: output {renewal_date:"2027-01-31", governing_law:"New York"} from contract text.

options.text: Knowledge Assistant
options.explanation: Incorrect. Knowledge Assistant is better for asking questions over documents, not producing a repeated structured table of fields. Example: “What is the termination clause?” is QA; extracting termination_notice_days for every contract is IE.

options.text: Supervisor Agent
options.explanation: Incorrect. A supervisor is useful for coordinating multiple agents/tools, not the simplest choice for one extraction task. Example: use a supervisor if contract extraction must also call a CRM and create tasks.

options.text: Classification
options.explanation: Incorrect. Classification assigns documents or messages to labels, while this scenario needs multiple structured fields from each contract. Example: label a contract as HighRisk is classification; extracting renewal_date and governing_law is information extraction.

questions.explanation: This tests task selection: structured fields from unstructured documents = information extraction.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A user request may require querying sales tables through Genie, searching public web information, and calling a ticketing API. Which architecture is most appropriate?

options.text: Supervisor Agent coordinating specialized tools/agents
options.explanation: Correct. A supervisor can delegate to different agents/tools and synthesize results. Example: ask Genie for internal sales totals, use web search for a public competitor event, then create a ticket.

options.text: Single embedding model with no tools
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embeddings can retrieve similar text but cannot query Genie, use web search, or call APIs. Example: a vector similarity lookup cannot create a Jira ticket.

options.text: One giant system prompt containing all future data
options.explanation: Incorrect. Static prompts are not appropriate for dynamic tools or current data. Example: next week’s sales and web news cannot be reliably embedded in one prompt today.

options.text: A single document-only RAG retriever
options.explanation: Incorrect. A document retriever can answer policy/document questions, but it cannot run Genie analytics or create CRM tickets. Example: retrieving a sales-policy PDF will not execute a SQL question or open a ticket.

questions.explanation: When a request spans multiple domains/actions, use an agent/supervisor pattern rather than a single static prompt.

questions.question: A restaurant wants to route chat messages into Reservation, Cancellation, Complaint, or Other. Which model task is the best fit?

options.text: Text classification
options.explanation: Correct. The output is one label from a fixed taxonomy. Example: “I need to cancel tonight” -> Cancellation.

options.text: Summarization
options.explanation: Incorrect. Summarization compresses text into a shorter text, not a fixed routing label. Example: “Customer wants to cancel” is useful, but the app needs a category.

options.text: Embedding generation only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embeddings can help similarity search but do not directly enforce a fixed class label. Example: you could retrieve similar examples, but still need a classifier or prompt for the label.

options.text: OCR
options.explanation: Incorrect. OCR extracts text from images/scans, not categories from already available chat text. Example: OCR would help if the request came as a scanned handwritten note.

questions.explanation: Fixed label set = classification. Do not confuse it with generation or retrieval.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: An assistant must answer “Can this customer return order X?” using order status, return-policy text, and customer tier. What tool order is most sensible?

options.text: Fetch order/customer facts, retrieve return-policy chunks, then ask the LLM to reason over both
options.explanation: Correct. The LLM needs both structured facts and policy context before generating a grounded answer. Example: order delivered 20 days ago + Gold tier + policy chunk about 30-day returns.

options.text: Ask the LLM first, then fetch order facts only if the user complains
options.explanation: Incorrect. The initial answer may hallucinate without needed facts. Example: the LLM cannot know order delivery date until a tool retrieves it.

options.text: Retrieve policy chunks but ignore order status and customer tier
options.explanation: Incorrect. The policy alone is insufficient because eligibility depends on order-specific fields. Example: a 30-day policy is useless without the delivery date.

options.text: Fine-tune a model on historical returns and avoid tools
options.explanation: Incorrect. Eligibility is dynamic and depends on current transactional data. Example: return status may change after the model was trained.

questions.explanation: Tool order should gather required structured and unstructured context before final generation.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A business requirement says: “Generate a short reason code for why each invoice was rejected, using invoice fields and rejection notes.” Which input/output description is best?

options.text: Input invoice fields plus rejection notes; output one reason code from an approved taxonomy plus a short explanation
options.explanation: Correct. It maps business data to a controlled output. Example: input vendor_id, amount, free-text note; output DuplicateInvoice with one-sentence rationale.

options.text: Input all company emails; output any helpful text the model wants
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is too broad and not aligned to the invoice rejection workflow. Example: emails from unrelated departments add noise and compliance risk.

options.text: Input invoice ID only; output a long natural-language essay
options.explanation: Incorrect. Invoice ID alone lacks the rejection notes and structured fields, and a long essay does not match reason-code reporting. Example: downstream analytics needs a code, not free prose.

options.text: Input rejection notes; output vector embeddings only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embeddings are intermediate representations; they are not the business-facing reason code. Example: a finance dashboard needs “MissingPO”, not a 768-dimensional vector.

questions.explanation: Exam questions often ask you to translate goals into precise pipeline inputs and outputs.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A prompt must extract purchase_order_id from emails. If the ID is absent, downstream systems require the JSON value to be null, not guessed. Which instruction should be included?

options.text: If purchase_order_id is not explicitly present, set purchase_order_id to null; do not infer it from surrounding text.
options.explanation: Correct. This prevents hallucinated IDs and creates a deterministic missing-value behavior. Example: “PO pending” should return {"purchase_order_id": null}.

options.text: If missing, invent the most likely purchase order ID based on vendor history.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This encourages hallucination and creates false operational records. Example: inventing PO-123 could route an invoice to the wrong purchase order.

options.text: Always return a string, even when no ID exists.
options.explanation: Incorrect. A placeholder string like "unknown" may violate the required schema and complicate downstream validation. Example: null is easier to distinguish from a real ID.

options.text: Ignore missing fields and return a natural-language apology.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The downstream system expects JSON, not conversational text. Example: an ETL parser will fail on “Sorry, I could not find it.”

questions.explanation: For extraction, explicitly define absence handling. “Do not guess” is a key guardrail for structured outputs.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: PDF policy documents are organized by numbered sections and subsections. Which chunking strategy is usually the best starting point for RAG?

options.text: Split on section/subsection boundaries, with modest overlap when needed
options.explanation: Correct. Structure-aware chunks preserve semantic units and make retrieved context easier for the LLM to use. Example: keep “2.3 Refund Exceptions” as one chunk rather than cutting it mid-rule.

options.text: Split every document into one giant chunk
options.explanation: Incorrect. Giant chunks can exceed context limits and reduce retrieval precision. Example: retrieving an entire 80-page policy for one refund question wastes context.

options.text: Split every 10 characters regardless of words or sections
options.explanation: Incorrect. Tiny character chunks destroy meaning and increase record count. Example: splitting “return window is 30 days” into fragments makes retrieval unusable.

options.text: Use only filenames as chunks
options.explanation: Incorrect. Filenames rarely contain enough answer content. Example: “HR_policy.pdf” cannot answer the actual maternity-leave rule.

questions.explanation: Chunk according to document structure and retrieval needs. Preserve enough context while avoiding huge noisy chunks.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A vector index is over the row limit. Quality is acceptable but record count is too high. Which change is most likely to reduce rows with least conceptual risk?

options.text: Slightly increase chunk size and reduce excessive overlap
options.explanation: Correct. This reduces chunk count while keeping related text together. Example: move from 300-token chunks with 200-token overlap to 600-token chunks with 80-token overlap.

options.text: Switch to a larger embedding dimension
options.explanation: Incorrect. Larger dimensions increase per-row storage and do not reduce row count. Example: 4096-dimensional vectors make each row heavier, not fewer.

options.text: Add a reranker
options.explanation: Incorrect. A reranker changes result ordering after retrieval, not how many records exist in the index. Example: reranking top 50 docs does not reduce a 150M-row index.

options.text: Increase overlap to improve continuity
options.explanation: Incorrect. More overlap usually creates more duplicate chunks and more rows. Example: high overlap may improve continuity but worsens the row-limit problem.

questions.explanation: Row count is controlled by chunking and overlap, while embedding dimension controls row size.

questions.question: Source documents are HTML pages and the goal is to extract text with minimal code. Which package is the most appropriate?

options.text: BeautifulSoup
options.explanation: Correct. BeautifulSoup parses HTML and extracts text/elements. Example: select article text from <main> or remove navigation/sidebar content.

options.text: pytesseract
options.explanation: Incorrect. pytesseract is OCR for images, not normal HTML. Example: use it for scanned PNGs, not web pages with HTML tags.

options.text: PyPDF2 or pypdf
options.explanation: Incorrect. PDF libraries parse PDFs, not HTML pages. Example: use pypdf for policy.pdf, not an article webpage.

options.text: NumPy
options.explanation: Incorrect. NumPy handles numerical arrays, not HTML parsing. Example: it can store embeddings later, but it will not extract text from tags.

questions.explanation: Match extraction tool to file type: HTML parser for HTML, OCR for images, PDF parser for PDFs.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A news RAG app should answer only technology questions, but the corpus includes sports ads and entertainment snippets. What is the best data-preparation action?

options.text: Filter irrelevant content upstream before indexing and/or at retrieval time
options.explanation: Correct. Removing or filtering noisy content improves retrieval precision before generation. Example: tag topic=technology and exclude topic=sports from the index/query.

options.text: Keep all content and rely only on the system prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. Prompts help, but noisy retrieval can still put irrelevant context in front of the LLM. Example: a sports chunk retrieved for “Apple” can distract the answer.

options.text: Increase the LLM temperature
options.explanation: Incorrect. Higher temperature increases randomness; it does not remove irrelevant source text. Example: a more creative answer may be less grounded.

options.text: Disable citations so irrelevant sources are not visible
options.explanation: Incorrect. Hiding citations masks the symptom and reduces trust. Example: users need to see that an answer came from relevant technology articles.

questions.explanation: RAG quality starts with good source preparation and retrieval filtering, not only prompt instructions.

questions.question: A DataFrame has one row per document and an array column containing all chunks. What layout is best before syncing to an AI Search index?

options.text: Flatten to one row per chunk with a stable unique chunk ID and metadata columns
options.explanation: Correct. Vector indexes typically expect each searchable chunk as its own record with metadata. Example: chunk_id, doc_id, section, text, updated_at.

options.text: Keep one row per document with an array of chunks
options.explanation: Incorrect. The retriever needs chunk-level records to retrieve the most relevant section. Example: a question about section 4 should not return the entire document array.

options.text: Store each chunk as a separate local JSON file only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Local files are not a governed, queryable Delta source for index sync. Example: a Delta table in Unity Catalog is easier to govern and sync.

options.text: Put all chunks into one string column for the whole corpus
options.explanation: Incorrect. One massive corpus string destroys retrieval granularity. Example: any query would retrieve the same giant text blob.

questions.explanation: Prepare chunked text as a Delta table with one row per retrievable unit plus metadata.

questions.question: A product-support RAG app must answer questions for a selected product_id and ignore other products with similar names. What should the index and query design include?

options.text: Text embeddings plus product_id metadata and a filter on product_id at query time
options.explanation: Correct. Metadata filtering limits retrieval to the selected product before or during semantic search. Example: filter product_id=SKU123 so the retriever does not return SKU124 documentation.

options.text: Only raw text without metadata
options.explanation: Incorrect. Semantic similarity alone can confuse related products. Example: two phone models with similar manuals may retrieve the wrong product.

options.text: Only product_id values without text embeddings
options.explanation: Incorrect. Exact IDs alone do not support semantic search within the product documentation. Example: after filtering to SKU123, you still need to find the warranty section.

options.text: A larger chat model instead of metadata filters
options.explanation: Incorrect. A stronger generator cannot fix wrong retrieved product context reliably. Example: if the prompt contains the wrong manual, the answer may still be wrong.

questions.explanation: Use metadata for exact constraints and embeddings for semantic matching inside the constrained set.

questions.question: You are comparing chunking strategies for a retriever using a labeled set of questions and relevant chunks. Which metric is most appropriate to evaluate ranking quality?

options.text: nDCG or recall@K on retrieved chunks
options.explanation: Correct. These retrieval metrics evaluate whether relevant chunks are retrieved and ranked well. Example: nDCG rewards putting the correct policy chunk at rank 1 instead of rank 8.

options.text: Training loss of the chat model
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chat-model training loss does not directly measure retriever ranking. Example: a low generation loss can still use irrelevant retrieved chunks.

options.text: BLEU between the user question and the chunk text
options.explanation: Incorrect. BLEU is n-gram overlap and is not a strong retrieval-ranking metric for semantic relevance. Example: “refund” and “return reimbursement” may be relevant but low overlap.

options.text: GPU memory used by the vector endpoint only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Memory is operational, not a relevance metric. Example: a cheap index can still return the wrong chunks.

questions.explanation: Retriever evaluation should focus on retrieval outcomes: recall, precision/ranking metrics, and relevance judgments.

questions.question: AI Search retrieves 50 candidates, but relevant documents often appear around ranks 20-30 and only the top 5 go to the prompt. What should you consider?

options.text: Increase generation temperature
options.explanation: Incorrect. Temperature changes generation randomness, not retrieved-document ordering. Example: the LLM still sees the wrong top 5 chunks.

options.text: Disable metadata filters
options.explanation: Incorrect. Removing filters may add more irrelevant candidates. Example: a product-specific question could start retrieving other products.

options.text: Use a PDF parser instead of an embedding model at query time
options.explanation: Incorrect. Parsing is an ingestion-time task; it does not reorder candidates during retrieval. Example: once indexed, ranking is handled by search/reranking.

questions.question: Your source documents are in a Delta table and should update the search index automatically as the table changes. Which index pattern is the best fit?

options.text: Direct Access index only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Direct access is managed directly by API operations rather than automatically synced from a Delta source. Example: use it when your app controls upserts/deletes explicitly.

options.explanation: Incorrect. Manual re-embedding can work for experiments but is not the best fit when a Delta table should keep the index updated. Example: a new document row should flow through the sync instead of relying on someone rerunning a notebook.

options.text: A model-serving traffic split
options.explanation: Incorrect. Traffic splits route requests between model versions; they do not sync document chunks from Delta to an AI Search index. Example: 90/10 champion-challenger routing does not update indexed docs.

questions.question: A support knowledge base changes every few minutes and users expect new articles to be searchable quickly. Cost matters but stale answers are unacceptable. What should drive the index configuration?

options.text: Update frequency and freshness requirements, not just initial index build cost
options.explanation: Correct. The index choice and sync settings should reflect how quickly changes must appear. Example: a support article published at 10:00 should be retrievable shortly after if agents rely on it.

options.text: Choose the largest embedding model regardless of update frequency
options.explanation: Incorrect. A larger model may improve quality but does not by itself solve freshness or sync cadence. Example: high-quality embeddings that update daily still miss articles from the last hour.

options.text: Avoid metadata columns because they slow development
options.explanation: Incorrect. Metadata often enables filtering, governance, and debugging. Example: article_id, product_id, and updated_at help filter and diagnose stale results.

options.text: Fine-tune the LLM whenever a new article is published
options.explanation: Incorrect. Fine-tuning for every article is costly and operationally unrealistic. Example: RAG index updates are the standard pattern for changing knowledge bases.

options.explanation: Incorrect. Publicly viewable data can still be copyrighted or license-restricted. Example: a website article may be readable but not reusable for training.

options.text: Use data first and notify curators only after launch
options.explanation: Incorrect. Permission should be resolved before use. Example: post-launch objections can force retraining/removal and create legal risk.

options.text: Rely on the model to forget restricted data automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. Models and datasets do not automatically enforce license terms. Example: restricted text can still influence outputs or evaluation data.

questions.explanation: Licensing is about permission and terms before use, not whether data is easy to download.

questions.question: Which measure is strongest against prompt injection that tries to force an agent to call dangerous tools?

options.text: Tool allow-lists, argument validation, least-privilege permissions, and output checks
options.explanation: Correct. Security controls should be enforced outside the LLM. Example: a refund tool only accepts order IDs belonging to the authenticated user.

options.text: A friendly system prompt saying “never do bad things” only
options.explanation: Incorrect. System prompts help but can be attacked; they are not a complete control. Example: a malicious document can contain “ignore previous instructions.”

options.text: More context chunks in every prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. More context can add more injection surface and noise. Example: retrieved web pages may contain hidden instructions.

options.text: Disable all traces and inference tables
options.explanation: Incorrect. Observability helps detect abuse; disabling it does not constrain tools. Example: traces show which tool was called and with what arguments.

questions.explanation: Agent security requires defense in depth: prompt rules plus real permission/tool enforcement.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A RAG app produces offensive answers because the indexed source documents include offensive forum comments. What is the best mitigation?

options.text: Curate/filter the upstream data before indexing and add output safety checks
options.explanation: Correct. Remove harmful source content and guard the generated output. Example: exclude abusive comments from the knowledge base before embedding.

options.text: Increase model max tokens
options.explanation: Incorrect. Longer answers may include more harmful content, not less. Example: a toxic retrieved chunk can be quoted in a longer response.

options.text: Tell users that offensive outputs are expected
options.explanation: Incorrect. Disclaimers do not mitigate harm or meet safety requirements. Example: a customer-facing app should prevent toxic content, not normalize it.

options.text: Use a smaller embedding model
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embedding size does not clean toxic source data. Example: the same harmful text can still be retrieved.

questions.explanation: For problematic source text, fix the data pipeline and apply safety guardrails; do not rely on user disclaimers.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A company policy bot must answer only from documents the current user is allowed to read. What design is most appropriate?

options.text: Permission-aware retrieval using governed tables/indexes and user/group access checks
options.explanation: Correct. Retrieval must respect access controls before context reaches the LLM. Example: HR salary docs are retrieved only for HR users with SELECT permission.

options.text: Retrieve everything, then ask the LLM not to reveal restricted facts
options.explanation: Incorrect. Restricted context already reached the model, creating leakage risk. Example: the model may paraphrase confidential text despite the instruction.

options.text: Store all documents in a public bucket
options.explanation: Incorrect. Public storage bypasses enterprise access control. Example: anyone with the URL could read restricted PDFs.

options.text: Use a higher-quality LLM and no permissions
options.explanation: Incorrect. Model quality does not enforce authorization. Example: GPT-level reasoning cannot replace UC privileges.

questions.explanation: Never pass unauthorized context to the model. Enforce access before retrieval/generation.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A prototype accidentally generated thousands of expensive model calls over a weekend. Which Databricks control helps prevent repeat runaway usage?

options.text: Configure AI Gateway rate limits on the serving endpoint/service
options.explanation: Correct. Rate limits cap query or token usage by endpoint/user/group. Example: set a default per-user QPM/TPM limit for development users.

options.text: Ask the LLM to refuse too many requests in the prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. The model cannot reliably enforce platform-level consumption limits. Example: every request still reaches the endpoint and incurs cost.

options.text: Remove all inference logging
options.explanation: Incorrect. Logging helps detect and investigate runaway usage; removing it does not cap calls. Example: usage tables can show who generated the cost.

options.text: Increase max tokens per request
options.explanation: Incorrect. That can increase cost, not control it. Example: a 4,000-token response is more expensive than a 500-token cap.

questions.explanation: Cost/abuse controls should be enforced at the endpoint/gateway level, not by prompt hope.

questions.question: A fine-tuned customer-facing model uses proprietary training data, and the company worries about unauthorized access and model inversion risk. Which Databricks mitigation is most relevant?

options.text: Restrict model access with ACLs/permissions and expose it only through governed endpoints
options.explanation: Correct. Access control reduces who can query the model and attempt extraction attacks. Example: only the customer-support app service principal can call the endpoint.

options.text: Publish the model artifacts publicly for transparency
options.explanation: Incorrect. Public artifacts increase risk to proprietary weights/data. Example: attackers could inspect or host the model themselves.

options.text: Disable all endpoint monitoring
options.explanation: Incorrect. Monitoring helps detect abnormal usage patterns. Example: many probing queries from one user could indicate extraction attempts.

options.text: Use a longer system prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. Prompt text alone cannot prevent unauthorized access or model extraction attempts. Example: an attacker can still send many probes if the endpoint is open.

questions.explanation: For proprietary models, governance and endpoint access controls are central risk mitigations.

questions.question: Which built-in judge requires ground-truth expectations?

options.text: Correctness
options.explanation: Correct. Correctness compares the response against expected/ground-truth information. Example: expected answer says the refund window is 30 days; the judge checks whether the response is correct.

options.text: RelevanceToQuery
options.explanation: Incorrect. Relevance evaluates whether the response addresses the user query and does not require a ground-truth answer. Example: a response about shipping is irrelevant to a billing question.

options.text: Safety
options.explanation: Incorrect. Safety checks harmful/offensive content and does not require a ground-truth answer. Example: flag toxic content in a response.

options.text: RetrievalGroundedness
options.explanation: Incorrect. Groundedness checks whether the answer is supported by provided context; it does not require a separate expected answer. Example: answer claims “60 days” when retrieved policy says “30 days.”

questions.explanation: Databricks built-in judges distinguish no-ground-truth dimensions such as relevance/safety/groundedness from correctness, which needs expectations.

questions.question: A RAG answer cites a retrieved document but adds a fact that is not present in the retrieved context. Which metric/judge is most directly relevant?

options.text: RetrievalGroundedness or faithfulness
options.explanation: Correct. This evaluates whether the generated response is supported by the retrieved context. Example: context says “return within 30 days” but answer says “60 days.”

options.text: Context recall only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Context recall asks whether needed information was retrieved; it does not by itself check unsupported generated claims. Example: the right chunk may be retrieved and the model can still hallucinate.

options.text: Endpoint QPS
options.explanation: Incorrect. QPS is an operational throughput metric, not factual support. Example: high QPS can coexist with hallucinated answers.

options.text: Embedding dimension
options.explanation: Incorrect. Dimension is a model/index property, not a generated-answer support metric. Example: 1024-dim embeddings do not prove the answer is grounded.

questions.explanation: Groundedness/faithfulness is the key concept for “answer must come from retrieved context.”

questions.question: What does Context Precision evaluate in RAG?

options.text: Whether relevant retrieved chunks are ranked ahead of irrelevant chunks
options.explanation: Correct. It measures ranking quality among retrieved context. Example: the refund-policy chunk should appear above a generic marketing paragraph.

options.text: Whether the final answer exactly matches a ground-truth string
options.explanation: Incorrect. Exact answer matching is answer-level correctness, not context precision. Example: two different phrasings can be correct.

options.text: Whether the model response is free of toxic content
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is a safety dimension. Example: a safe answer can still use poorly ranked context.

options.text: How many GPUs the endpoint uses
options.explanation: Incorrect. GPU count is infrastructure, not retrieval ranking. Example: a larger endpoint does not guarantee relevant chunks are ranked first.

questions.explanation: Precision-style retrieval metrics focus on relevance/noise and ordering of retrieved chunks.

questions.question: What does Context Recall evaluate in RAG?

options.text: Whether the retrieved context contains the information needed to answer the question
options.explanation: Correct. Recall asks whether required facts were retrieved at all. Example: if the answer needs shipping date and carrier, both should appear in retrieved context.

options.text: Whether irrelevant chunks are ranked after relevant chunks
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is closer to context precision/ranking. Example: recall can be high even if relevant chunks are ranked low.

options.text: Whether the answer is polite
options.explanation: Incorrect. Politeness is a style/guideline dimension, not context recall. Example: a polite answer can still miss the needed source document.

options.text: Whether the LLM uses fewer output tokens
options.explanation: Incorrect. Token length is cost/latency, not retrieval completeness. Example: a short answer can be incomplete because the retriever missed the key chunk.

questions.explanation: Recall is about missing necessary evidence. Precision is about avoiding/ranking irrelevant evidence.

questions.question: What are inference tables used for in Databricks AI Gateway/model serving monitoring?

options.text: Logging requests and responses to Unity Catalog Delta tables for monitoring, debugging, and optimization
options.explanation: Correct. Inference tables capture serving payload/metadata for analysis. Example: inspect prompts/responses that caused low-quality ratings.

options.text: Creating embeddings for documents
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embeddings are generated by embedding models; inference tables store serving logs. Example: use an embedding endpoint to vectorize chunks, not inference tables.

options.text: Replacing all access controls
options.explanation: Incorrect. Logging does not replace permissions. Example: you still need endpoint and data access controls.

options.text: Training the base LLM automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. Inference logs can inform evaluation/fine-tuning, but they do not automatically train the model. Example: use logs to build an evaluation dataset first.

questions.explanation: Inference tables are observability data: requests/responses stored for analysis and monitoring.

questions.question: Which feature helps track token usage, latency, users, and cost consumption for AI Gateway services?

options.text: AI Gateway usage tracking system table
options.explanation: Correct. Usage tracking records operational usage such as token usage and latency. Example: query system.ai_gateway.usage to see which team generated the most tokens.

options.text: Chunk overlap
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chunk overlap affects retrieval chunks, not account-level usage tracking. Example: changing overlap can affect cost indirectly, but does not report usage.

options.text: pytesseract
options.explanation: Incorrect. pytesseract extracts text from images; it does not track endpoint cost. Example: OCR a scanned invoice before indexing.

options.text: Model card license field
options.explanation: Incorrect. Licensing metadata helps legal compliance, not live usage accounting. Example: license terms say whether you may use a model, not how many tokens users consumed.

questions.explanation: For cost/usage monitoring, look for usage tables and gateway metrics, not retrieval preprocessing settings.

questions.question: Before using Lakehouse Monitoring dashboards on GenAI inference logs, what preparation is often needed?

options.text: Flatten/unpack nested request and response payloads into structured columns
options.explanation: Correct. Monitoring works best when fields such as prompt, response, latency, status, and tokens are columns. Example: parse JSON payloads into prompt_text and generated_answer.

options.text: Convert all text to images
options.explanation: Incorrect. Images make text monitoring harder, not easier. Example: monitoring answer length needs text columns.

options.text: Delete timestamps to avoid drift analysis
options.explanation: Incorrect. Time fields are needed for monitoring trends and drift. Example: compare response latency this week vs last week.

options.text: Store logs only in a local CSV on your laptop
options.explanation: Incorrect. Lakehouse monitoring expects governed tables in Databricks, not local private files. Example: use a Unity Catalog Delta table.

questions.explanation: Inference logs often contain nested JSON. Flatten the fields you want to monitor.

questions.question: When should you use a code-based custom scorer rather than an LLM judge?

options.text: When the criterion is deterministic, such as valid JSON schema or exact field presence
options.explanation: Correct. Code is reliable for strict, machine-checkable rules. Example: assert that every response has keys ticket_id, category, confidence.

options.text: When evaluating nuanced helpfulness with many valid phrasings
options.explanation: Incorrect. Nuanced judgments often need an LLM judge or human rubric. Example: “Was this answer empathetic?” is not simple exact matching.

options.text: When you want to avoid defining any metric
options.explanation: Incorrect. A scorer still requires a metric definition. Example: a JSON schema scorer needs the schema.

options.text: When there is no application output to evaluate
options.explanation: Incorrect. A scorer needs inputs/outputs/traces to score. Example: you cannot score a response that was never generated.

questions.explanation: Use deterministic code scorers for deterministic requirements; use LLM judges for semantic quality.

questions.question: How can Databricks production monitoring evaluate GenAI quality after deployment?

options.text: Schedule MLflow scorers on sampled traces from the production app
options.explanation: Correct. Production monitoring can run scorers on traces to assess quality over time. Example: sample 5% of support-agent traces and score groundedness.

options.text: Ask every end user to manually grade every answer before they see it
options.explanation: Incorrect. Human feedback is valuable but grading every answer blocks the user experience and does not scale. Example: sample and review strategically.

options.text: Only compare model parameter counts
options.explanation: Incorrect. Parameter count is not a production quality metric. Example: a smaller model with better retrieval can outperform a larger one.

options.text: Turn off tracing after deployment
options.explanation: Incorrect. Traces are needed for debugging and scorer-based monitoring. Example: without traces, you cannot inspect which tool caused an error.

questions.explanation: Use the same or similar scorers across development evaluation and production monitoring when possible.

questions.question: What is the best reason to create an evaluation dataset for a GenAI app before changing prompts or retrievers?

options.text: It lets you compare versions consistently and detect regressions
options.explanation: Correct. A stable evaluation set gives a repeatable benchmark. Example: test prompt v2 against the same 100 tricky customer questions as v1.

options.text: It guarantees the app will pass the real certification exam
options.explanation: Incorrect. Evaluation datasets help app quality, not certification outcomes. Example: strong app eval still requires studying exam objectives.

options.text: It removes the need for human review forever
options.explanation: Incorrect. Human/SME feedback may still be needed to validate metrics and edge cases. Example: new policy ambiguity may require SME judgment.

options.text: It makes retrieval unnecessary
options.explanation: Incorrect. Evaluation measures the app; it does not replace retrieval. Example: a RAG app still needs relevant context.

questions.explanation: Evaluation datasets support controlled iteration and regression testing.

questions.question: A customer-facing LLM endpoint has stable correctness scores but complaints about slow responses during peak hours. Which metrics are most relevant to monitor first?

options.text: Latency, request volume, error rate, and token usage over time
options.explanation: Correct. The problem is operational performance under load. Example: p95 latency spikes at 10:00 when request volume doubles.

options.text: Only answer correctness
options.explanation: Incorrect. Correctness is stable and does not explain slowness. Example: a correct answer arriving after 20 seconds can still fail the SLA.

options.text: Only embedding recall@K
options.explanation: Incorrect. Retrieval recall may affect answer quality, but the complaint is response time. Example: recall@K=0.9 says nothing about p95 latency.

options.text: Only license metadata for the model
options.explanation: Incorrect. Licensing matters for compliance, not diagnosing latency spikes. Example: the model license will not show queueing delay.

questions.explanation: Monitoring depends on the scenario: quality issue -> quality metrics; speed/cost issue -> operational metrics.

questions.question: A RAG chain has already retrieved relevant chunks and now needs a final user-facing answer. Which component should be called next?

options.text: A chat/completion model with the retrieved context and user question in the prompt
options.explanation: Correct. Chat/completion models generate natural-language answers. Example: prompt the model with refund-policy chunks and ask for a cited answer.

options.text: The embedding model again to write the answer
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embedding models convert text to vectors for search/similarity; they do not compose final prose. Example: use embeddings before retrieval, not after retrieval to answer.

options.text: A reranker as the final answer generator
options.explanation: Incorrect. A reranker reorders candidate chunks; it does not generate the final answer. Example: rerank top 50 chunks, then send top 5 to the chat model.

options.text: The AI Search index as the final answer generator
options.explanation: Incorrect. The index returns records/chunks, not a synthesized response. Example: AI Search can return the warranty paragraph; the LLM turns it into an answer.

questions.explanation: This version keeps options in the same RAG pipeline family: embedding, retrieval, reranking, generation. The correct next component after retrieval is the generator LLM.

questions.question: You want to manage access, logging, and rate limits for calls to a third-party hosted LLM through Databricks. Which endpoint type/pattern fits best?

options.text: External model/service endpoint through Databricks serving governance
options.explanation: Correct. External model endpoints let Databricks manage access/governance around third-party model calls. Example: route OpenAI/Anthropic-style calls through a governed Databricks service endpoint.

options.text: Delta Sync index
options.explanation: Incorrect. Delta Sync creates/syncs a search index from Delta data; it does not proxy third-party LLM calls. Example: use it for document retrieval, not external model governance.

options.text: OCR pipeline
options.explanation: Incorrect. OCR extracts text from scans and is unrelated to LLM endpoint governance. Example: OCR contract images before extraction.

options.text: Prompt-only API-key hiding
options.explanation: Incorrect. Putting an API key in a prompt or frontend is not governance. Example: use endpoint configuration/secrets and access controls instead.

questions.explanation: External model serving is the Databricks pattern for governing calls to models hosted outside Databricks.

questions.question: A custom pyfunc RAG model fails in serving because a package installed interactively in the notebook is missing at endpoint runtime. What should be fixed?

options.text: Declare/package the model dependencies when logging the model
options.explanation: Correct. Serving needs reproducible dependencies captured with the model. Example: include langchain, databricks-sdk, or pydantic versions in the logged environment.

options.text: Increase chunk overlap
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chunk overlap affects retrieval data, not Python package availability. Example: no amount of overlap installs a missing import.

options.text: Change answer relevancy metric
options.explanation: Incorrect. Metrics evaluate quality; they do not fix runtime imports. Example: a scorer cannot import a missing dependency for the endpoint.

options.text: Use a longer prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. Prompt length does not install packages. Example: ImportError must be fixed in environment/dependency packaging.

questions.explanation: Packaging dependencies is a deployment concern; notebook state is not enough for reproducible serving.

questions.question: What is the clearest difference between tracing and aggregate monitoring?

options.text: Tracing shows the step-by-step execution for individual requests; monitoring summarizes behavior over time
options.explanation: Correct. Tracing is per-request observability, while monitoring tracks trends/metrics. Example: a trace shows a failed tool call; monitoring shows error rate increased this week.

options.text: Tracing is only for training classical ML models
options.explanation: Incorrect. MLflow tracing is specifically useful for GenAI chains and agents. Example: trace a LangChain retriever and LLM call.

options.text: Monitoring means the app no longer needs logs
options.explanation: Incorrect. Monitoring is built from logs/traces/metrics. Example: inference tables can feed dashboards.

options.text: They are identical names for the same feature
options.explanation: Incorrect. They are related but operate at different granularity. Example: trace one bad answer, monitor p95 latency over a day.

questions.explanation: Use traces for debugging a specific request; use monitoring for production trends.

questions.question: A model keeps adding an explanation after a requested one-line summary. Which prompt change is most likely to fix the format issue?

options.text: Add explicit output instructions and a few examples showing only the desired one-line summary
options.explanation: Correct. Few-shot examples and clear constraints guide format. Example: “Return exactly one sentence. Do not include analysis.” followed by examples.

options.text: Increase chunk overlap
options.explanation: Incorrect. The issue is output format, not retrieval continuity. Example: retrieved news chunks may be fine; the prompt needs stricter format control.

options.text: Use OCR on the output
options.explanation: Incorrect. OCR reads images; it does not change model response style. Example: the answer is already text.

options.text: Delete the evaluation dataset
options.explanation: Incorrect. Removing evaluation makes the problem harder to measure and does not fix the model behavior. Example: keep test cases to verify the new prompt works.

questions.explanation: When the answer content is good but the format is wrong, improve prompt instructions/examples or add output parsing/validation.

questions.question: What does Answer Relevancy evaluate?

options.text: Whether the generated response addresses the user’s original question intent
options.explanation: Correct. It checks query-response alignment. Example: user asks about refund deadline; answer about shipping cost is not relevant.

options.text: Whether the retrieved context contains every ground-truth fact
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is retrieval sufficiency/recall style evaluation, not answer relevancy. Example: missing a policy exception is a context issue.

options.text: Whether the model used the fewest possible tokens
options.explanation: Incorrect. Token count is cost/latency, not relevancy. Example: a short answer can still answer the wrong question.

options.text: Whether the response exactly copies the retrieved text
options.explanation: Incorrect. Copying is not required; the answer can paraphrase and still be relevant/grounded. Example: summarize the policy in plain language.

questions.explanation: Relevancy is about answering the question asked, not whether every fact is correct or every retrieved chunk was good.

questions.question: An insurance chatbot must refuse political questions and respond with a standard message because company policy limits the bot to insurance topics. Which guardrail type best describes this?

options.text: Compliance/policy guardrail
options.explanation: Correct. The restriction comes from company policy about allowed topics. Example: “Sorry, I can only answer insurance questions” for election-related prompts.

options.text: Safety guardrail
options.explanation: Incorrect. Safety guardrails target harmful, toxic, or dangerous content. Example: blocking self-harm instructions is safety, not just off-topic politics.

options.text: Security guardrail
options.explanation: Incorrect. Security guardrails protect systems/data/tools from misuse. Example: blocking prompt injection that tries to export customer records.

options.text: Contextual relevance guardrail only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Contextual guardrails keep responses grounded or on-context, but the explicit driver here is a company policy/compliance boundary. Example: refusing non-insurance topics enforces policy, not just retrieval relevance.

questions.explanation: Guardrail labels overlap in practice, but exam-style questions usually key on the main risk: safety harm, security abuse, compliance/policy, or contextual grounding.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: Users search product docs with exact error codes like E102 and natural-language descriptions. Which retrieval mode is a strong candidate?

options.text: Hybrid search combining keyword/full-text and vector similarity
options.explanation: Correct. Hybrid search can capture exact terms like error codes plus semantic meaning. Example: E102 must match exactly, while “device will not start” benefits from vectors.

options.text: Vector search only with no keyword signal
options.explanation: Incorrect. Pure vector search can miss exact codes or identifiers. Example: E102 may be treated as an arbitrary token.

options.text: Keyword search only with no semantic signal
options.explanation: Incorrect. Keyword search can miss paraphrases. Example: “cannot power on” and “will not start” may need semantic matching.

options.text: A reranker without initial retrieval
options.explanation: Incorrect. Rerankers need a candidate set first. Example: retrieve top 50 with hybrid search, then rerank.

questions.explanation: When queries contain exact identifiers and natural language, hybrid retrieval is often a good starting point.

questions.question: A JSON extraction chain sometimes returns different field names for the same input. Which change is most relevant?

options.text: Lower temperature and enforce a schema/parser
options.explanation: Correct. Lower randomness and schema validation improve consistency. Example: require keys order_id, date, sender_email every time.

options.text: Increase temperature for creativity
options.explanation: Incorrect. Higher temperature usually increases variability. Example: it may output “purchaseOrder” instead of “order_id”.

options.text: Remove examples from the prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. Examples help the model learn the required structure. Example: one valid JSON example can reduce format drift.

options.text: Use only a vector index
options.explanation: Incorrect. A vector index retrieves context; it does not enforce output schema. Example: extraction still needs generation/parsing.

questions.explanation: For structured outputs, combine prompt constraints, lower randomness, and validation/parsing.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: A production app should always load the approved model version without hardcoding version 17. Which UC model-registry feature helps?

options.text: Model alias such as Champion
options.explanation: Correct. Aliases let the app refer to a role rather than a fixed version. Example: load model@Champion and repoint the alias after validation.

options.text: Chunk metadata field
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chunk metadata helps retrieval filtering, not model promotion. Example: product_id metadata does not choose model versions.

options.text: OCR engine
options.explanation: Incorrect. OCR extracts image text, unrelated to model lifecycle. Example: use OCR before indexing scanned docs.

options.text: Embedding overlap
options.explanation: Incorrect. Overlap affects document splitting, not version routing. Example: model version 17 vs 18 is handled by registry aliases.

questions.explanation: Aliases support promotion and rollback without changing application code.

questions.question: Why are BLEU/ROUGE limited for evaluating open-ended GenAI answers?

options.text: They focus on n-gram overlap and can miss semantically correct paraphrases
options.explanation: Correct. Text overlap metrics can penalize valid answers with different wording. Example: “30-day return window” and “returns allowed within one month” may be equivalent.

options.text: They require no reference text and always judge factuality
options.explanation: Incorrect. They usually compare against reference text and do not prove factual correctness. Example: high overlap can still copy an incorrect reference.

options.text: They measure endpoint latency
options.explanation: Incorrect. BLEU/ROUGE evaluate text similarity, not serving performance. Example: p95 latency is a separate operational metric.

options.text: They evaluate vector index permissions
options.explanation: Incorrect. Permissions are governed by access controls, not n-gram metrics. Example: SELECT privilege is not measured by ROUGE.

questions.explanation: For open-ended GenAI, semantic judges and human rubrics often complement or replace pure n-gram overlap.

questions.question: A team wants inference logging but must avoid storing raw personal data. What is the best pattern?

options.text: Log required metadata and redact/mask sensitive payload fields according to policy
options.explanation: Correct. This balances observability and privacy. Example: store latency, status, token counts, and a redacted prompt.

options.text: Log every raw prompt and response forever
options.explanation: Incorrect. This can create privacy and retention risk. Example: raw medical or customer PII should not be kept unnecessarily.

options.text: Disable all observability permanently
options.explanation: Incorrect. This removes debugging, audit, and quality-monitoring capability. Example: you could not investigate a harmful output.

options.text: Put secrets inside the prompt so logs capture them
options.explanation: Incorrect. Secrets should never be placed in prompts/logs. Example: API keys belong in secrets/env configuration.

questions.explanation: Good governance is not “no logs”; it is safe, intentional logging with access, masking, and retention controls.

questions.question: An LLM judge disagrees with SMEs on many borderline answers. What should the team do?

options.text: Align/calibrate the judge with SME feedback and refine the rubric
options.explanation: Correct. Judge alignment improves consistency with human standards. Example: update criteria for what counts as a complete insurance answer.

options.text: Ignore SMEs and trust the judge forever
options.explanation: Incorrect. SMEs define domain quality; the judge should be calibrated, not blindly trusted. Example: legal nuance may require expert labels.

options.text: Delete borderline examples from the evaluation set
options.explanation: Incorrect. Borderline cases are valuable for improving the system. Example: ambiguous policy exceptions reveal model weaknesses.

options.text: Use only latency metrics
options.explanation: Incorrect. Latency says nothing about semantic quality. Example: a fast but wrong answer still fails.

questions.explanation: SME feedback should improve rubrics, judges, and evaluation data rather than be ignored.

questions.question: When should you consider a custom MCP server rather than a managed or external one already available?

options.text: When the required tool/data source is unique to your organization and no suitable managed/external MCP server exists
options.explanation: Correct. Custom MCP is for custom capabilities. Example: expose an internal pricing engine with company-specific authentication and actions.

options.text: Always, because custom servers are lower maintenance than managed servers
options.explanation: Incorrect. Managed servers usually reduce maintenance. Example: do not rebuild a managed Databricks integration without a reason.

options.text: When you only need to split text into chunks
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chunking is data preparation, not MCP server integration. Example: use a splitter before indexing docs.

options.text: When you want to replace all evaluation metrics

options.text: A text embedding model
options.explanation: Incorrect. Embeddings turn text into vectors and do not transcribe audio. Example: use embeddings after the transcript exists.

options.text: A SQL warehouse
options.explanation: Incorrect. SQL can query transcript tables but does not transcribe audio. Example: query call duration after transcription.

options.text: A reranker
options.explanation: Incorrect. A reranker orders retrieved text chunks and does not handle audio input. Example: rerank transcript chunks after they are text.

questions.explanation: Select models by modality and task: audio transcription requires an audio/speech model.
