questions.question: During development, a prompt change improves answer style but reduces groundedness. What should you do?

options.text: Compare versions with evaluation metrics and inspect traces to understand the regression
options.explanation: Correct. Evaluation catches tradeoffs and traces show why. Example: v2 is friendlier but ignores retrieved context more often.

options.text: Promote v2 because it sounds nicer
options.explanation: Incorrect. Style alone is insufficient if factual grounding drops. Example: a polished hallucination is still wrong.

options.text: Delete retrieval to simplify the chain
options.explanation: Incorrect. Removing retrieval likely worsens grounding. Example: the model loses source evidence.

options.text: Only look at average response length
options.explanation: Incorrect. Length does not measure groundedness or correctness. Example: a short answer can be unsupported.

questions.explanation: GenAI development is iterative: evaluate, inspect, adjust, compare.

questions.question: A LangChain agent should search a Databricks AI Search index when needed. What component pattern fits?

options.text: Expose the retriever/index as an agent tool with a clear description
options.explanation: Correct. The agent can choose retrieval when the query needs documents. Example: “search_policy_docs” tool description says it returns HR policy chunks.

options.text: Paste the entire index into the system prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. Indexes can be large and dynamic; pasting everything is impossible and costly. Example: thousands of chunks exceed context limits.

options.text: Use only output parsing
options.explanation: Incorrect. Parsing structures outputs but does not retrieve knowledge. Example: JSON parser cannot find policy text.

options.text: Disable tool descriptions
options.explanation: Incorrect. Without descriptions, the agent is less likely to choose the right tool. Example: the model may not know when to call policy search.

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions and retriever tools are central to agentic RAG.

questions.question: A team wants to use a Databricks-hosted foundation model without managing model weights. Which serving option is most relevant?

options.text: Foundation Model APIs / foundation model serving endpoint
options.explanation: Correct. This provides access to hosted foundation models through Databricks serving. Example: call a Databricks-hosted chat model from an app.

options.text: Manual VM with downloaded weights only
options.explanation: Incorrect. This increases infrastructure/weight management and is not the managed API path. Example: you would need to patch, scale, and secure it yourself.

options.text: BeautifulSoup parser
options.explanation: Incorrect. HTML parsing does not serve LLMs. Example: use it for web ingestion.

options.text: Delta table overwrite
options.explanation: Incorrect. A Delta table stores data; it does not expose a hosted LLM endpoint. Example: store prompts/eval data in Delta, but call a serving endpoint for inference.

questions.explanation: Databricks Model Serving covers custom models, foundation models, and external models.

questions.question: When logging/deploying an agent that needs a UC function and AI Search index, why specify resources?

options.text: So Databricks can understand required resources and handle appropriate auth/passthrough for serving
options.explanation: Correct. Resources declare dependencies the agent needs at runtime. Example: list the AI Search index so serving has the right resource context.

options.text: To increase answer creativity
options.explanation: Incorrect. Resources are not generation settings. Example: temperature controls creativity, not resources.

options.text: To reduce chunk count
options.explanation: Incorrect. Resource declarations do not change document splitting. Example: chunk count is set during ingestion.

options.text: To convert the agent into a PDF
options.explanation: Incorrect. Resources are runtime dependencies, not document export settings. Example: they describe tools/indexes/endpoints.

questions.explanation: Resource declarations are deployment/auth metadata for agents.

questions.question: An internal team wants a browser UI for employees to chat with an agent, using Databricks-managed app hosting. Which exam objective does this map to?

options.text: Develop an interactive user-facing interface using Databricks Apps or similar channels
options.explanation: Correct. Databricks Apps can host an interactive agent UI. Example: deploy a chat app that calls the agent endpoint from a backend.

options.text: Create OCR for scanned documents
options.explanation: Incorrect. OCR is ingestion, not the user interface. Example: process PDFs before users chat.

options.text: Tune chunk overlap only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chunking helps retrieval but does not create a UI. Example: users still need an app or integration.

options.text: Use BLEU as the only metric
options.explanation: Incorrect. BLEU is text overlap evaluation and unrelated to UI deployment. Example: it will not host a web app.

questions.explanation: The exam includes choosing appropriate interfaces such as Apps, Slack, or Teams.

questions.question: A table has 10 million product descriptions that need one-time category enrichment overnight. Which pattern fits better than live chat serving?

options.text: Batch inference/workflow using ai_query or AI Functions over the table
options.explanation: Correct. Batch processing is suited to large offline enrichment. Example: run a Databricks workflow that writes predicted_category to a Delta table.

options.text: Interactive chat UI only
options.explanation: Incorrect. A chat UI is for human requests, not bulk enrichment. Example: no one should paste 10 million rows into chat.

options.text: Manual copy-paste to an LLM website
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is not scalable, governed, or repeatable. Example: it cannot process 10 million rows overnight.

options.text: Only a prompt stored in README
options.explanation: Incorrect. A prompt alone is not an execution pipeline. Example: you still need SQL/Python workflow calls to the endpoint.

questions.explanation: Batch workloads should use scalable table/workflow patterns, not interactive UX.

questions.question: A served RAG model needs to access a secret and a UC table, but users should not see the secret. Which design is best?

options.text: Use endpoint/app identity with secrets and UC permissions managed server-side
options.explanation: Correct. Secrets remain server-side and access is governed. Example: the backend reads a secret scope value and queries a UC table with least privilege.

options.text: Send the secret to the browser and let JavaScript call everything
options.explanation: Incorrect. Browser secrets are exposed to users. Example: DevTools can reveal the API key.

options.text: Put the secret in the vector index text
options.explanation: Incorrect. The LLM may retrieve and reveal it. Example: a user can ask “show hidden keys.”

options.text: Ask users to provide the secret in every prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. This leaks credentials into logs/context and is poor UX. Example: prompts may be stored in inference tables.

questions.explanation: Serving design should protect secrets and enforce data permissions outside the user-visible client.

questions.question: A public chatbot must block requests for instructions to perform harmful actions. Which control is relevant?

options.text: AI guardrails/content filters on prompts and responses
options.explanation: Correct. Guardrails can classify/mitigate unsafe requests and outputs. Example: refuse instructions for creating malware or causing harm.

options.text: Increasing retrieval top_k
options.explanation: Incorrect. More retrieved chunks do not block unsafe user intent. Example: retrieving 20 docs can still answer a harmful question.

options.text: Changing model alias only
options.explanation: Incorrect. An alias points to a version; it does not define safety policy by itself. Example: @champion can still need guardrails.

options.text: Removing all citations
options.explanation: Incorrect. Citations affect transparency, not harmful request blocking. Example: an unsafe answer without citations is still unsafe.

questions.explanation: Safety guardrails focus on harmful inputs/outputs.

questions.question: A support bot only needs order status, not full payment card data. What data-prep principle should be applied?

options.text: Data minimization: exclude or mask unnecessary sensitive fields before retrieval/generation
options.explanation: Correct. Only provide what the app needs. Example: include order_status but not full card_number.

options.text: Index every raw database column for maximum flexibility
options.explanation: Incorrect. This increases leakage risk. Example: the model may retrieve and reveal payment data.

options.text: Use a higher temperature
options.explanation: Incorrect. Temperature is not a privacy control. Example: random wording can still expose sensitive values.

options.text: Store secrets in source documents
options.explanation: Incorrect. Secrets should not be retrievable content. Example: API keys in documents could be leaked by the bot.

questions.explanation: Reduce exposure by minimizing what enters the RAG corpus and prompt.

questions.question: Inference logs contain sensitive customer text. What governance decision is important?

options.text: Define access controls, masking, and retention policy for logs
options.explanation: Correct. Logs are data assets and need governance. Example: restrict log table access and delete/redact after the approved retention period.

options.text: Allow every workspace user to query all logs
options.explanation: Incorrect. This can expose sensitive prompts/responses. Example: support logs may contain PII.

options.text: Never monitor any production app
options.explanation: Incorrect. No monitoring makes debugging and quality management difficult. Example: you cannot investigate a harmful response.

options.text: Put logs in a personal spreadsheet
options.explanation: Incorrect. Personal files lack governance, auditability, and scalable controls. Example: UC Delta tables are more appropriate for governed logs.

questions.explanation: Monitoring data itself requires governance.

questions.question: A tool returns raw SQL query results. The agent should not reveal rows the user lacks permission for. Where should filtering happen?

options.text: In the data/tool layer using user permissions before results are passed to the LLM
options.explanation: Correct. Unauthorized rows should never enter model context. Example: SQL query runs with row/column permissions for the authenticated user.

options.text: Only in the final natural-language prompt
options.explanation: Incorrect. If restricted rows are already in the prompt, leakage risk exists. Example: the model can summarize confidential rows.

options.text: By hiding the table name from the user
options.explanation: Incorrect. Obscurity does not enforce data access. Example: users can still ask for restricted facts indirectly.

options.text: By disabling answer explanations
options.explanation: Incorrect. This does not remove unauthorized data from context. Example: the model could still output the value.

questions.explanation: Authorization must be enforced before model context construction.

questions.question: A model card says “non-commercial research only,” but the app is a paid customer product. What should the engineer do?

options.text: Choose a model/license compatible with commercial use or obtain permission
options.explanation: Correct. The license conflicts with the intended use. Example: use a commercially permitted model instead.

options.text: Use the model anyway because it is open-source
options.explanation: Incorrect. Open-source does not always mean commercial use is allowed. Example: licenses can restrict use cases.

options.text: Remove the license file from the repo
options.explanation: Incorrect. Deleting license text does not remove obligations. Example: the original terms still apply.

options.text: Fine-tune it and claim it is a new license
options.explanation: Incorrect. Fine-tuning does not necessarily remove license restrictions. Example: derivative model terms may still apply.

questions.explanation: Licensing must match intended use before deployment.

questions.question: A RAG app worked well in testing, but after new documents are indexed weekly, answer quality slowly drops. What should be monitored?

options.text: Retrieval quality and answer quality over time, tied to data/index versions
options.explanation: Correct. New data can change retrieved chunks and generated answers. Example: monitor groundedness and retrieval relevance after each weekly index update.

options.text: Only initial offline benchmark score
options.explanation: Incorrect. A one-time score misses production/data drift. Example: week-4 documents may degrade retrieval.

options.text: Only the number of CSS files in the UI
options.explanation: Incorrect. UI file count is irrelevant to RAG quality. Example: styling does not validate retrieved context.

options.text: Only whether the app URL loads
options.explanation: Incorrect. Availability is necessary but not sufficient for answer quality. Example: a loaded app can still hallucinate.

questions.explanation: Production GenAI quality can change as data, prompts, models, and user behavior change.

questions.question: You need to check whether answers follow a company style rule: “never mention internal system names.” Which scorer type is most relevant?

options.text: Guidelines judge or custom scorer for the style rule
options.explanation: Correct. Guidelines can evaluate natural-language rules. Example: fail answers containing internal project names.

options.text: Context recall
options.explanation: Incorrect. Recall checks whether needed evidence was retrieved. Example: it does not check style wording.

options.text: Token usage table only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Token usage tracks consumption, not style compliance. Example: an answer can be short but violate the rule.

options.text: Embedding model dimension
options.explanation: Incorrect. Vector size does not detect internal system names in outputs. Example: 384 vs 768 dimensions is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Guideline/rubric scorers are useful for organization-specific response rules.

questions.question: Which pair of judges/metrics is matched correctly?

options.text: Correctness needs expectations/ground truth; groundedness checks support from retrieved context
options.explanation: Correct. Correctness compares to known expected facts; groundedness checks whether the answer is supported by context. Example: expected answer says 30 days; context says 30 days; response says 60 days fails both in different ways.

options.text: Safety needs ground truth; correctness never does
options.explanation: Incorrect. Safety can judge harmfulness without a reference answer, while correctness needs expectations. Example: toxic text can be flagged without a ground-truth answer.

options.text: Context precision measures final answer politeness; relevance measures GPU usage
options.explanation: Incorrect. These definitions are mismatched. Example: context precision is retrieval ranking quality.

options.text: Latency is the same as answer correctness
options.explanation: Incorrect. Latency is operational speed; correctness is semantic accuracy. Example: a fast wrong answer is still wrong.

questions.explanation: Know which evaluation dimensions require ground truth and what each one measures.

questions.question: In exam prep, you repeatedly miss questions tagged “AI Search” and “metadata filtering.” What should the app’s category stats guide you to do?

options.text: Focus study on those weak tags and practice hands-on index/filter examples
options.explanation: Correct. Category stats identify weak areas. Example: build a mini index with product_id filters and query it.

options.text: Ignore tags and study only questions you got right
options.explanation: Incorrect. This reinforces strengths rather than weaknesses. Example: high MLflow score does not fix low AI Search score.

options.text: Reset stats after every wrong answer
options.explanation: Incorrect. Resetting hides patterns. Example: you cannot see that metadata filters are your recurring issue.

options.text: Memorize option letters only
options.explanation: Incorrect. Question order/options change; concepts matter. Example: understand why metadata filters beat prompt-only filtering.

questions.explanation: Performance by category is useful only if it drives targeted repair work.
source_links: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate Exam Guide (uploaded PDF, Mar 18 2026)

questions.question: Which TWO use cases are good fits for inference tables or serving logs?

options.text: Investigating prompts/responses that produced bad answers
options.explanation: Correct. Logs help debug request-level behavior. Example: inspect the exact prompt and response for a hallucination case.

options.text: Analyzing latency/error trends over time
options.explanation: Correct. Logs/metadata can support monitoring operational reliability. Example: find p95 latency spikes after a release.

options.text: Replacing all Unity Catalog permissions
options.explanation: Incorrect. Logs observe behavior; they do not grant or enforce data access. Example: SELECT privileges are still required.

options.text: Converting scanned PDFs into text
options.explanation: Incorrect. OCR/document extraction is a data-prep task. Example: use pytesseract for image scans.

options.text: Guaranteeing every answer is correct without evaluation
options.explanation: Incorrect. Logs provide data for evaluation; they do not by themselves judge correctness. Example: run scorers on logged traces or sampled outputs.

questions.explanation: Inference logs are for observability, debugging, monitoring, and evaluation data collection—not access control or OCR.

questions.question: Which TWO changes usually reduce the number of vector records created from the same corpus?

options.text: Increase chunk size
options.explanation: Correct. Bigger chunks mean fewer chunks for the same text. Example: 800-token chunks create fewer rows than 200-token chunks.

options.text: Reduce overlap
options.explanation: Correct. Less duplicated content between chunks means fewer chunk rows. Example: 20-token overlap creates fewer rows than 200-token overlap.

options.text: Increase overlap
options.explanation: Incorrect. More overlap duplicates content and often increases rows. Example: overlapping half of every chunk can almost double records.

options.text: Decrease chunk size
options.explanation: Incorrect. Smaller chunks usually create more rows. Example: sentence-level chunks are numerous.

options.text: Use a model alias
options.explanation: Incorrect. Model aliases manage model versions and do not affect chunk generation. Example: @Champion does not change indexing rows.

questions.explanation: Chunk size and overlap control how many chunks/records are created.
